American Expansion. The rapid territorial growth of the United States from independence through the late nineteenth century, driven by ideology, economics, and demographics. The nation's expansion westward—from the Atlantic to the Pacific—displaced Native Americans, defined Manifest Destiny, and shaped American identity.

It began with the Louisiana Purchase in eighteen oh-three, which doubled the nation's size. The acquisition from France cost fifteen million dollars and opened the interior to American settlement. The Lewis and Clark Expedition from eighteen oh-four to eighteen oh-six explored the new western territories, gathering geographic and anthropological knowledge that facilitated subsequent settlement.

Manifest Destiny became the dominant ideology—the belief that American expansion to the Pacific was inevitable and righteous. It provided justification for westward pressure. But this expansion came at great cost. Indian Removal policies, culminating in the Indian Removal Act of eighteen thirty and the Trail of Tears, forcibly relocated tens of thousands of Native Americans.

The Mexican-American War from eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight brought vast southwestern territories into the US, including present-day California, Nevada, Utah, and Arizona. The Oregon Territory settlement with Britain in eighteen forty-six extended American sovereignty to the Pacific Northwest, completing continental expansion. Settlement accelerated through the Homestead Act of eighteen sixty-two, which offered free land to settlers, and the transcontinental railroad, completed in eighteen sixty-nine.

This process reshaped the continent's political boundaries, intensified sectional tensions over slavery, and established the continental United States.
